diagnosis:
All three settled rollouts (0, 1, 2) share the same pattern: PF1 and PF2 are both revealed and cited in justification_fact_ids, and the settlements' decisions clearly reflect the facts' content (staffed indoor gallery, no online gallery, student initials, 7-year retention, district records archive). Yet checks C1, C3, C5, C6, C7, C8, and P1 all fail in every settled rollout while C2, C4, and P2 pass. This is not a disclosure problem (facts are revealed), not a telepathy problem (facts are cited and the values match), and not a misapplied problem (the settlements correctly apply the revealed information). The issue is ENCODING MISMATCH: the checks that fail (C1, C3, C5, C6, C7, C8, P1) are looking for field names or value strings that the model does not naturally produce in the settlement, while the checks that pass (C2, C4, P2) match what the model does produce.

Specifically, across all three settled rollouts the settlement decisions object contains: display_venue (string), online_gallery (boolean false), label_policy (string like 'Student initials only...' or 'student initials'), original_retention_years (7), and archive_location (string). Checks C4 (passed) validates original_retention_years=7 and C2 (passed) validates online_gallery=false — these align with the model's field names. P2 (passed) checks PF2 provenance. But C1, C3, C5, C6, C7, C8, and P1 all fail, meaning the checks that are supposed to validate the venue (C1), label policy (C3), retention period (C5), archive location (C6, C7), spoken-restrictions commitment (C8), and PF1 provenance (P1) are either checking field names that don't match what the model writes (e.g., expecting a different field name than 'display_venue', 'label_policy', 'archive_location'), or are checking for commitment types that the model doesn't produce (e.g., 'spoken-restrictions' or 'privacy-protocol' commitment types — the model instead uses 'revision', 'revision_assignment', 'plan_revision', 'records_update', 'approval', 'final_approval').

For the single auto-failed rollout (index 3, turn cap 10): both PF1 and PF2 were revealed by turns 2–3, and by turn 8 all substantive discussion was complete. The conversation continued with A3 repeating agreement at turns 8–9 without A1 issuing a settle action. The unparsable model output at turn 3 did not block the conversation — the remaining turns parsed fine. The failure to settle is a structural problem: A1 (the facilitator/approver) never issued a settle action even though all facts were surfaced and consensus was reached by turn 8. Raising the turn cap alone would not reliably fix this — A1 needs clearer settle-eligibility prompting or the settle-eligibility condition needs loosening so that settled-after-consensus is achievable within the cap.
